This paper presents a broad empirical study of task-specific knowledge distillation for natural language generation under a practically motivated setting: medium-resource labeled data, additional unlabeled task-specific inputs, off-the-shelf pretrained models, and a strong emphasis on inference efficiency. The central technical focus is on pseudo-target (PT) training, extending standard sequence-level KD by using multiple PTs, sampling-based PT generation, PTs on unlabeled inputs, and a new “Joint-Teaching” method that mixes teacher- and student-generated PTs while applying word-level KD. The paper also includes architectural comparisons between encoder-decoder and decoder-only models, pruning analyses, and a small-scale “extreme setup” using GPT-4 as teacher without task-specific teacher fine-tuning.

Overall, I found the paper interesting, practically relevant, and stronger as a systematic empirical study than as a sharply isolated methodological contribution. The work addresses an important gap: much of the KD literature for NLP either focuses on NLU, generic LM compression, or high-resource settings, whereas many real deployments indeed have modest labeled data and abundant unlabeled task-specific inputs. The paper’s main message—that PT-based augmentation is substantially more effective than the conventional single beam-generated pseudo-target recipe, especially when unlabeled data is available—is useful and likely actionable for practitioners. The proposed Joint-Teaching idea is also intuitively appealing and empirically promising.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the breadth and coherence of the empirical investigation. The authors do not just propose one new trick; they walk through a sequence of design decisions and quantify their effects across four English-to-English generation tasks and two teacher-student pairs. The findings are fairly consistent and practically meaningful: encoder-decoder models outperform decoder-only models for these conditional generation tasks; decoder pruning is preferable to encoder pruning when latency matters; combining logits KD with PT training is better than either alone; unlabeled inputs help substantially when converted into PT supervision; multiple PTs are better than a single PT; and sampling-based PT generation is better than beam-based mode approximation in this setting. These are useful conclusions, and the inclusion of latency and throughput alongside FLOPs and parameter counts is a real strength.

I also appreciated the paper’s attempt to connect PT training to exposure bias. The argument that PTs expose the student to non-gold prefixes and therefore partially reduce the train-test mismatch is sensible, and the Joint-Teaching method is a natural extension of that perspective. The motivating analysis in Figure 2 is not definitive, but it does provide some evidence that the teacher can better continue student prefixes than the student itself during training. This makes the method more than a purely heuristic recipe.

That said, I have several concerns about the paper’s methodology and the strength of some of its claims.

First, the paper is framed as a “systematic study,” but the experimental design is sequential and greedy rather than factorial. At each stage, one choice is fixed based on average dev performance and then subsequent decisions are explored conditioned on that choice. This is understandable computationally, and the authors are transparent about it, but it limits the strength of the conclusions. Interactions between choices may be substantial: for example, the best PT decoding strategy may depend on whether logits KD is used, on the student architecture, or on whether unlabeled PTs are included. Likewise, Joint-Teaching may interact with the number or diversity of PTs. Because the study does not evaluate these interactions systematically, some of the “recipe” conclusions should be interpreted as conditional rather than general. I would encourage the authors to soften the universality of the recommendations or add targeted interaction experiments.

Second, the aggregation and reporting methodology in Table 3 is somewhat hard to interpret and occasionally obscures absolute performance. Reporting “fraction of the student-teacher gap closed” is reasonable as a normalization, but it can be unstable or misleading when the teacher-student gap is small, when metrics have different scales, or when a student surpasses the teacher. The paper also averages this quantity across metrics and across two teacher-student pairs, which may hide important heterogeneity. Since the paper’s main contribution is empirical, I would strongly prefer more emphasis in the main text on absolute task metrics for each dataset and pair, not only normalized gap closure. Table 4 helps for the final models, but the intermediate conclusions would be easier to trust if absolute numbers and variance were more visible.

Third, statistical reliability is not sufficiently addressed. The paper reports many comparisons across tasks, metrics, and methods, but I did not see confidence intervals, standard deviations over random seeds, or significance testing. Given that some dev-score differences are small (e.g., 16.0 vs 15.9 vs 15.9 in Table 3A), it is difficult to know whether the stage-wise selections are robust. This is especially important because the paper’s conclusions are often based on modest average improvements accumulated over many design choices. At minimum, the final comparisons and key ablations should be repeated over multiple seeds.

Fourth, the novelty of some components is moderate. Multiple PTs, unlabeled-data pseudo-labeling, and sampling-based augmentation are natural extensions of sequence-level KD rather than fundamentally new techniques. That is not a fatal issue for a systems/empirical paper, but it means the paper’s contribution rests heavily on careful experimentation and convincing analysis. In that regard, the exposure-bias framing is interesting but still somewhat speculative. The paper claims this is the first work to discuss exposure bias in KD, but the actual evidence that the gains arise specifically from exposure-bias mitigation rather than simply from data augmentation or better coverage of teacher outputs is limited. Joint-Teaching is the most novel element, but even there the mechanism is not fully disentangled. For example, is the gain due to conditioning on student prefixes, due to regularization from mixed PT sources, or simply due to more diverse training sequences? Additional ablations would help.

Fifth, the comparison between encoder-decoder and decoder-only models is potentially confounded. The paper concludes that encoder-decoder architectures outperform decoder-only ones for task-specific conditional NLG, which may well be true in this regime, but the compared model families differ in pretraining objectives, tokenization, optimization history, and adaptation format. The authors acknowledge some of this in the appendix, but the main-text claim is still stronger than the evidence strictly supports. I would phrase this more carefully as an empirical observation for the chosen off-the-shelf families and tasks, rather than a general architectural conclusion.

Sixth, the pruning study is useful but narrow. Only one pruning strategy is considered, only BART-6:6 is pruned, and the pruning is layer dropping with a fixed heuristic of keeping first and last layers. The conclusion that decoder pruning is better than encoder pruning is plausible and likely useful, but again should be scoped to this setup. It would be stronger with at least one alternative pruning ratio or one learned pruning baseline.

Seventh, the “realistic setup” is somewhat selective. The paper argues that several thousand labeled examples plus abundant unlabeled inputs is realistic, which is fair, but one of the datasets uses 40K labeled examples, which is not obviously “several thousand.” More broadly, the tasks are all English-to-English and mostly relatively short-output conditional generation tasks. The authors acknowledge this in limitations, but the title and framing could still lead readers to overgeneralize. I would encourage clearer scoping in the abstract and conclusion.

Eighth, the GPT-4 extreme setup is interesting but underdeveloped. The results are described as mixed, and the explanation is attributed to tokenizer mismatch, but this remains speculative. Since this section is not the main contribution, that is acceptable, but the paper should be careful not to overstate transferability of the main findings to frontier-model distillation. In particular, the inability to test Joint-Teaching there weakens the narrative that the proposed recipe generalizes broadly.

There are also some evaluation concerns specific to the chosen tasks and metrics. For style transfer/simplification, lexical overlap metrics can be imperfect proxies for style fidelity and meaning preservation. For abductive reasoning, automatic metrics are especially noisy, and while the human evaluation in the appendix is helpful, it would be better if the main text more explicitly acknowledged the limitations of BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore for that task. Similarly, perplexity on gold targets is not always aligned with generation quality, especially when training on PTs that may differ systematically from references. The paper does use multiple metrics, which is good, but some discussion of metric validity per task would strengthen the evaluation section.

A few additional clarifications would improve the paper. I would like to know more precisely how many PTs are used in each stage, whether the total number of student update steps is controlled across methods, and whether gains from multiple PTs persist when controlling for total token budget rather than total examples. As written, some improvements may partly reflect simply more training data or more optimization steps. Similarly, for unlabeled PTs, it would be useful to compare against using the same number of additional labeled PTs or against self-training baselines without KD to isolate the source of gains. For Joint-Teaching, the 50/50 mixing ratio seems arbitrary; a sensitivity analysis would be valuable.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper makes a meaningful contribution. The empirical findings are useful, the practical orientation is refreshing, and the PT-focused study is likely to be valuable to researchers and practitioners working on efficient task-specific generation. The paper is especially compelling if evaluated as a careful recipe paper rather than a theory-heavy methodological breakthrough. Its main weakness is that some conclusions are broader than the evidence warrants, and the experimental methodology would benefit from stronger controls and statistical rigor.

My recommendation is moderately positive. I would support acceptance if the venue values practical empirical studies and model compression for NLG, but I do think the paper would benefit from revisions that tighten claims and strengthen the evidence around key conclusions.

The most important improvements I would suggest are the following. First, add multi-seed results with variance for the main comparisons, especially Table 3 stage selections and final models. Second, include more absolute performance tables in the main paper, not only normalized gap-closure summaries. Third, add at least a few interaction ablations, such as whether sampling still beats beam when controlling for number of PTs and training budget, and whether Joint-Teaching still helps when PT diversity is matched. Fourth, clarify whether improvements from multiple PTs and unlabeled PTs are controlled for total training tokens/steps. Fifth, soften claims about architectural superiority and exposure-bias causality unless stronger evidence is added.

In summary, this is a solid and useful empirical paper with a good practical message: pseudo-target training for NLG distillation is more powerful than the standard single beam-generated PT recipe, especially when one leverages unlabeled task-specific inputs and diverse PT generation, and Joint-Teaching appears to further help. The work is not fully definitive, but it is thoughtful, relevant, and likely to influence how practitioners approach task-specific KD for generation.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper presents a broad empirical study of task-specific knowledge distillation for natural language generation under a medium-resource setting with additional unlabeled data. It compares encoder-decoder vs. decoder-only architectures, encoder vs. decoder pruning, several KD objectives, and a family of pseudo-target (PT) augmentation strategies. The main proposed method, Joint-Teaching, combines word-level KD with PTs generated by both teacher and student, motivated by exposure bias. Experiments span four English NLG tasks and two teacher-student pairs, with additional exploratory results on distilling GPT-4 in a label-scarce setting. The paper reports that encoder-decoder models are preferable for conditional NLG, decoder pruning is better than encoder pruning, unlabeled-data PTs help substantially, multiple sampled PTs outperform single beam PTs, and Joint-Teaching yields the best average gap-closing performance.
strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: compressing NLG models for deployment while leveraging unlabeled task-specific data.
The study is unusually broad, covering architecture choice, pruning, KD objectives, PT generation strategies, and a new Joint-Teaching variant across multiple tasks.
The empirical setup includes practical efficiency metrics such as latency and throughput, not just parameter counts or FLOPs.
The pseudo-target analysis is thoughtful and extends standard sequence-level KD in several meaningful directions: unlabeled inputs, multiple PTs, and sampling-based PT generation.
The proposed Joint-Teaching idea is intuitive and practically motivated by exposure bias, and the reported gains over teacher-only or student-only PT training are promising.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear stage-wise experimental design and explicit practical recommendations for practitioners.
Including an exploratory extreme setup with GPT-4 broadens the relevance and highlights limitations of transferring the recipe to frontier-model teachers.
weaknesses: The work is framed as a systematic study, but the stage-wise greedy selection procedure means later conclusions depend on earlier choices and do not isolate interaction effects between design decisions.
Many central claims rely on averages over heterogeneous tasks and metrics, which can obscure instability or trade-offs; some conclusions appear weaker when inspecting task-specific behavior.
The proposed exposure-bias justification is suggestive rather than rigorous; the evidence for the causal mechanism behind PT diversity and Joint-Teaching is limited.

The empirical comparisons do not appear to include variance estimates, statistical significance tests, or multiple random seeds, making it hard to assess robustness of often small dev-score differences.

The evaluation relies heavily on automatic metrics such as BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore/PPL, which are imperfect for several studied generation tasks; human evaluation is only briefly mentioned for one dataset.
The paper introduces a new Shake7 dataset, but the main text provides limited detail on its construction, quality control, and potential overlap/bias issues, making it harder to assess validity.
The GPT-4 extreme setup is too limited to support strong conclusions and is confounded by prompt design, tokenizer mismatch, and restricted task coverage.
methodological_flaws: The sequential experimental design is a methodological limitation: selecting one option at each stage based on dev performance and then fixing it for subsequent stages can produce path-dependent conclusions. A method that loses early may interact favorably with later PT strategies, so claims of overall superiority are not fully justified.

The main aggregate metric, percentage of student-teacher gap closed, can be misleading and unstable across metrics with different scales and directions. In particular, averaging gap-closure percentages over BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, and PPL is not obviously meaningful, and values can behave oddly when the teacher-student gap is small or when a student surpasses the teacher.

The paper makes causal claims about exposure bias mitigation, but the supporting evidence is weak. Figure 2 only shows one setup and does not establish that the observed gains from PT sampling or Joint-Teaching arise specifically from reduced exposure bias rather than generic data augmentation or regularization.

The comparison between encoder-decoder and decoder-only architectures is not fully controlled. Models differ not only in architecture but also in pretraining objectives, tokenization, scaling histories, and implementation ecosystems, so attributing gains primarily to architecture is scientifically overstated.

The pruning conclusion is based on a single pruning scheme applied only to BART-6:6 by dropping layers while keeping first/last layers. This is too narrow to support a general claim that decoder pruning is better than encoder pruning beyond this specific model family and pruning heuristic.

The paper does not report uncertainty estimates or repeated runs. Given that several stage decisions are based on small dev-score differences (e.g., Logits vs. Noisy KD), the absence of variance analysis weakens empirical validity and may affect the selected recipe.

The use of unlabeled data may introduce distributional advantages not disentangled from the KD method itself. Since the paper does not compare against strong semi-supervised or self-training baselines without teacher logits/PTs, the gains cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed KD innovations.

The GPT-4 distillation section is methodologically underpowered: only two tasks, limited sample sizes, and unavailable comparison to Joint-Teaching. As a result, it cannot substantiate transferability claims of the main findings to the extreme setup.
